answer.rationale: Inheriting c2 (low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply last year with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing) and c4 (renegotiation at renewal recovered real margin via benchmarking) suggests that switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor is the most direct lever to deliver the 18% mandated cut. To respect c3’s lesson about avoiding a single point of failure while I still hold only one action this cycle, I will scope this as a small, guarded switch on the component c2 covered (rather than flipping the full book). This keeps the incumbent contract in place as a known-good fallback if the new vendor falters, which preserves delivery confidence for the 94% utilization line that has no buffer. The 14-day expiry creates the trigger point: rather than a like-for-like renewal, use this renewal window to redirect the eligible volume, and carry c4 into the negotiation with the incumbent to claw back margin on whatever footprint remains. I’m not yet committing to 'switch_primary_vendor' as the single memory pull; I’m requesting verification of c2 and c4 because (a) c2 anchors the cost case for switching and (b) c4 frames whether renegotiation with the incumbent could close part of the 18% gap on its own — if c4 shows renegotiation alone can hit ~10–12% on the incumbent book, I may blend ‘switch’ + ‘negotiate_terms’ rather than commit purely to switching. If the archive returns c2 with any caveat about quality, lead time, or volume scalability beyond what is summarized, I will pivot to 'negotiate_terms' with the incumbent, since the line running at 94% with no buffer means a swap failure is unacceptable. The current 14-day expiry makes 'defer_decision' costly (loss of negotiating leverage and possible service lapse), so it is not preferred despite c5’s prior success — that earlier deferral was a non-critical renewal, whereas this is primary supply at high utilization.
